mainTopic: רבי אבא's rulings to רב יוסף בר חמא: retracting an offered oath, collecting debts from slaves, testimony of relatives, and a witness who went blind
overview: This amud is a series of rulings that רבי אבא sent to רב יוסף בר חמא. First, if someone holding a slave tells the claimant 'swear and take him' and the claimant swears, the holder cannot back out. The גמרא asks why this is new, since a משנה in סנהדרין already teaches this about accepting unfit judges. It answers that the dispute in that משנה covers even an 'I will give you' case, and that the הלכה follows the חכמים. Next, רבי אבא rules that creditors collect from slaves, and רב נחמן disagrees. Then he rules that a third-generation relative may testify about a second-generation one. רבא extends this to third with first, and the הלכה rejects מר בר רב אשי's ruling allowing testimony about a grandfather. Finally, רבי אבא disqualifies a witness who went blind from testifying about land. שמואל, רב ששת and רב פפא allow him for land, a cloak and even silver, and the גמרא challenges them with a ברייתא saying a witness must be fit both when he sees the event and when he testifies. The answer to this challenge comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Once the claimant swears, the holder cannot back out
steps.stepSummary: This finishes רבי אבא's ruling. The holder of a slave tells the claimant to swear and take him, and once the claimant swears, the holder cannot retract.
steps.simpleTranslation: The holder says: 'You gave him to me as a gift. If you want, swear and take him.' If the claimant then swears, the holder cannot take back his offer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ruling of רבי אבא that began just before this section. Someone holding a slave offers to let the claimant take an oath and take the slave, and the claimant swears.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The holder did not have to make this offer, because he claims the slave is his. Even so, once the other side has acted on the offer and sworn, the holder is stuck with his word and cannot retract.

keyTerms.meaning: to back out of what he said

phrases.english: You gave him to me as a gift.
If you wish, swear and take him.
And he swore. He cannot retract.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a ruling of רבי אבא that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once the claimant swears at the holder's offer, the holder cannot back out.

steps.title: Why teach this? A משנה already says it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רבי אבא adds, since a משנה already rules that someone who accepts unfit judges cannot back out.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is he teaching us? We already learned this. If one side said, 'My father is trusted to judge for me,' or 'Your father is trusted,' or 'Three cattle herders are trusted,' רבי מאיר says he can back out and the חכמים say he cannot.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אבא's ruling as unnecessary. It points to an existing משנה that seems to teach the very same idea.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In that משנה, a person agrees to be judged by people who are normally unfit, such as relatives or unlearned herders. The חכמים say he cannot back out. Accepting an oath is the same idea: you agree to a way of deciding that you did not have to accept. So why did רבי אבא need to say it?

keyTerms.meaning: What is this teaching us? (asked when a ruling seems already known)
he is trusted by me (as a judge)
cattle herders, people who don't know הלכה

phrases.english: What is he teaching us?
We already learned: if he said to him:
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in סנהדרין 24a.

phrases.english: "My father is trusted to judge for me";
"Your father is trusted to judge for me";
"Three cattle herders are trusted to judge for me":

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: יָכוֹל לַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ,
phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says: he can retract,

phrases.aramaic: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ!
phrases.english: and the Rabbis say: he cannot retract!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 1 as already taught in a משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה in סנהדרין already teaches that someone who accepts an unusual way of deciding a case cannot back out, so רבי אבא seems to add nothing.

steps.title: The dispute covers 'I will give you,' and the הלכה follows the חכמים
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא teaches two new things. The dispute in the משנה also covers a case where the person must hand something over, and the הלכה follows the חכמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he teaches us: the dispute is even in a case of 'I will give you,' and the הלכה follows the חכמים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי אבא's ruling does add something. It shows how far the dispute in the משנה reaches, and it decides the הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think the משנה only covers a case where the person would just give up a debt owed to him. Here the holder would have to actually hand over a slave, which is an 'I will give you' case. רבי אבא shows the חכמים still say he cannot back out, and he rules like them.

keyTerms.meaning: this is what he is teaching us
"I will give you": a case where he must pay or hand something over

steps.whatToRemember: Even when someone would have to hand something over ('I will give you'), once he accepts an unusual way of deciding the case, such as unfit judges or the other side's oath, he cannot back out. The הלכה follows the חכמים.

phrases.english: This is what he teaches us:
that the dispute applies even to "I will give you,"
phrases.notes: Here he would have to actually hand something over, not just let go of money owed to him, like handing over the slave.

phrases.english: and the halakha follows the words of the Rabbis.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies a new detail plus a ruling on the הלכה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dispute in the משנה might only cover giving up a debt, and the הלכה was not yet decided.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dispute also covers 'I will give you' cases, and the הלכה follows the חכמים: he cannot back out.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Someone who accepts the other side's oath, or unfit judges, cannot back out, even when he must hand something over.

steps.title: רבי אבא rules that creditors collect from slaves
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא sends another ruling to רב יוסף בר חמא: creditors may collect a debt from slaves.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא sent to רב יוסף בר חמא: the הלכה is that creditors collect from slaves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic, another ruling that רבי אבא sent. It is about whether a debt can be collected by taking slaves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Debts are normally collected from land, and the heirs of a man who died owe his debts out of the land he left them. רבי אבא rules that slaves count like land for this purpose, so creditors can take them.

keyTerms.meaning: he sent to him (a ruling by message)

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba sent to
Rav Yosef bar Ḥama:
The halakha is: they collect from the slaves.
phrases.notes: He means creditors of a man who died can take the slaves he left to his heirs.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא לְרַב יוֹסֵף בַּר חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling sent by the same רבי אבא, on a different topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Creditors may collect debts from slaves.

steps.title: רב נחמן says creditors do not collect from slaves
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן disagrees with רבי אבא and rules that debts are not collected from slaves.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב נחמן said: they do not collect from slaves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings an opposing opinion. רב נחמן says creditors cannot take slaves to pay a debt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבא treats slaves like land, so creditors can collect from them. רב נחמן does not allow collecting from slaves. The גמרא records both opinions and moves straight on to the next ruling רבי אבא sent.

phrases.english: And Rav Naḥman said: they do not collect.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite ruling to step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Debts are not collected from slaves.

steps.title: Third generation testifying about second generation is valid
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא sends a ruling that a third-generation relative may testify about a second-generation relative.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא sent to רב יוסף בר חמא: The הלכה is that a third-generation relative testifying about a second-generation relative is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ruling that רבי אבא sent, this time about which relatives may testify for each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Generations are counted down from a shared ancestor: his children are the first generation, his grandchildren the second, and his great-grandchildren the third. A third-generation witness and a second-generation relative are far enough apart that the witness is not disqualified as a relative. A first cousin once removed is an example.

keyTerms.meaning: Third generation from the shared ancestor
Second generation from the shared ancestor

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba sent
to Rav Yosef bar Ḥama:
The halakha is: a third-generation relative testifying about a second-generation one is valid.
phrases.notes: Count the generations down from the ancestor they share. For example, a person may testify about his father's first cousin.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא לְרַב יוֹסֵף בַּר חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another item in the series of rulings רבי אבא sent, on a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Testimony of a third-generation relative about a second-generation relative is valid.

steps.title: רבא allows third generation about first generation
steps.stepSummary: רבא says that even a third-generation relative testifying about a first-generation relative is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא says: Even third testifying about first is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds to רבי אבא's ruling and makes the permission wider.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבא only spoke about third with second. רבא says the gap between third and first is also enough. For example, a person may testify about his great-uncle.

keyTerms.meaning: First generation from the shared ancestor

phrases.english: Rava says: Even with regard to the first.
phrases.notes: He means a third-generation witness may testify even about a first-generation relative.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends רבי אבא's ruling to a wider gap between generations.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Testimony of a third-generation relative about a first-generation relative is also valid.

steps.title: מר בר רב אשי allows testimony about a grandfather
steps.stepSummary: מר בר רב אשי ruled that a person may testify about his father's father.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בר רב אשי ruled that testimony about one's father's father is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports a practical ruling by מר בר רב אשי that applied רבא's idea to a grandfather.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מר בר רב אשי treated a grandson and grandfather like third and first generation, following רבא's rule. That made him think the grandson could testify.

phrases.english: Mar bar Rav Ashi
ruled testimony valid with regard to a father's father;

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי אַכְשַׁר בְּאַבָּא דְאַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבא's rule to a grandson and grandfather.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A grandson may testify about his grandfather.

steps.title: The הלכה does not follow מר בר רב אשי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rules that the הלכה is not like מר בר רב אשי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The הלכה is not in accordance with מר בר רב אשי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes this topic by rejecting מר בר רב אשי's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though רבא allows third about first, that does not cover a grandson and his own grandfather. A grandfather remains a relative who may not be testified about.
steps.whatToRemember: Third about second is valid (רבי אבא), and רבא allows third about first. But a grandson may not testify about his grandfather.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume that 'third about first' means grandson and grandfather. The הלכה rejects that application.

phrases.aramaic: וְלֵית הִלְכְתָא כְּמָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי.
phrases.english: But the halakha is not in accordance with Mar bar Rav Ashi.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵית הִלְכְתָא כְּמָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the ruling in the previous step.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Testimony about one's grandfather is invalid.

steps.title: A witness to land who became blind is disqualified
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא rules that someone who knew testimony about a field and then went blind may not testify.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא sent to רב יוסף בר חמא: If a person knew testimony about land before he became blind, and then he became blind, he is disqualified.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling from רבי אבא about a witness who saw the facts while he could see but is now blind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The witness knew where the field's borders were while he could still see. רבי אבא rules that once he is blind he can no longer testify about it.

keyTerms.meaning: Testimony about land, such as its borders

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba sent
to Rav Yosef bar Ḥama:
If one knew testimony for another about land
before he became blind,
and then he became blind, he is disqualified.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא לְרַב יוֹסֵף בַּר חָמָא: הָיָה יוֹדֵעַ לוֹ בְּעֵדוּת קַרְקַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling from רבי אבא on a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A witness who became blind is disqualified from testifying about land.

steps.title: שמואל allows a blind witness for land boundaries
steps.stepSummary: שמואל disagrees and says the blind witness is fit for land, but not for a cloak.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: He is fit, since he can still figure out the boundaries. But for a cloak he is not fit.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל argues with רבי אבא and allows the blind witness to testify about land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל holds that a blind person can still determine exactly where a field's boundaries are, so his earlier knowledge remains usable. A cloak, though, is a movable item, and שמואל holds a blind person cannot identify it.

keyTerms.meaning: That he can figure out exactly

phrases.english: And Shmuel said: He is fit,
since it is possible that he can determine its boundaries.
But a cloak, no.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A blind witness may testify about land boundaries, but not identify a cloak.

steps.title: רב ששת allows a blind witness even for a cloak
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת says the blind witness can identify even a cloak by its size, but not a piece of silver.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: Even a cloak, since he can figure out its length and width. But a piece of silver, no.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת goes one step further than שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A cloak can be identified by measuring its length and width, which a blind person can do by touch. A piece of silver has no such clear signs, so רב ששת does not allow it.

keyTerms.meaning: A piece or bar of silver

phrases.english: And Rav Sheshet said: Even a cloak,
since it is possible that he can determine
its length and its width.
But a piece of silver, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends שמואל's leniency from land to a cloak.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A blind witness may identify a cloak by its size, but not a piece of silver.

steps.title: רב פפא allows a blind witness even for silver
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the blind witness can identify even a piece of silver by its weight.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Even a piece of silver, since he can figure out its weight.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא goes the furthest and allows the blind witness to identify even a piece of silver.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Silver has no length and width to go by, but it has a weight. A blind person can feel or check the weight, so רב פפא allows it.
steps.whatToRemember: The opinions go step by step: רבי אבא disqualifies a blind witness. שמואל allows him for land. רב ששת allows him for a cloak too. רב פפא allows him even for silver.

phrases.english: And Rav Pappa said: Even a piece of silver,
since it is possible that he can determine its weight.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends רב ששת's leniency from a cloak to silver.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A blind witness may identify even a piece of silver by its weight.

steps.title: A ברייתא says a witness who went blind is disqualified
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל with a ברייתא. It says that a witness who could see when he saw the event and then went blind is פסול.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: If a person knew testimony for someone before he became that person's son-in-law, and then he became his son-in-law; or he could hear and then became deaf; or he could see and then went blind; or he was sane and then went insane, he is disqualified.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא to attack שמואל, who said a witness who went blind can still testify about land. The ברייתא lists cases where a witness saw something while fit and later became unfit, and rules that he cannot testify.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One of the cases in the list is פיתח ונסתמא, someone who could see and then went blind. The ברייתא calls him פסול, which clashes directly with שמואל. It also clashes with רב ששת and רב פפא, who built on שמואל's ruling, and it fits רבי אבא's view.

keyTerms.meaning: His son-in-law, a relative who cannot testify
Someone who can see (his eyes are open)

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
If he knew testimony about him
before he became his son-in-law,
and then he became his son-in-law;
or he could hear, and then became deaf;
or he could see, and then went blind;
or he was sane, and then went insane: he is disqualified.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's ruling, and the rulings of רב ששת and רב פפא that build on it.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling (step 11) that a witness who went blind is fit to testify about land.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא explicitly lists 'could see and then went blind' as a case of פסול, with no exception for land.

steps.title: The ברייתא continues: if the problem went away, he is fit
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds that if the disqualifying problem ended before he testified, the witness is כשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he knew testimony for him before he became his son-in-law, then became his son-in-law, and then his daughter died; or he could hear, became deaf, and then could hear again; or he could see, went blind, and then could see again; or he was sane, went insane, and then became sane again, he is fit.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא keeps going and gives the flip side. If the problem disappeared before the witness came to court, he may testify.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each case from the first list is repeated, but now the problem goes away. The daughter dies, so the family tie ends, or the hearing, sight, or sanity comes back. This shows that being unfit in the middle period does not ruin the testimony, as long as he is fit again when he testifies.

keyTerms.meaning: And his daughter died, so the family tie ends
And then went back to his earlier state

phrases.english: But if he knew testimony about him
before he became his son-in-law,
and then he became his son-in-law, and then his daughter died;
or he could hear, became deaf, and then could hear again;
or he could see, went blind, and then could see again;
or he was sane, went insane, and then became sane again: he is fit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, giving the contrasting cases where the witness is fit.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only when sight comes back is the witness כשר. That implies a witness who stays blind remains פסול.

steps.title: The ברייתא's rule: fit at the start and at the end
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא sums up: if a witness was unfit either when he saw the event or when he testifies, he is פסול. Only if he was fit at both times is he כשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the rule: anyone whose beginning or end is in a state of disqualification is disqualified. If his beginning and end are both in a state of fitness, he is fit.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives one general rule that explains all the cases above. It finishes the source the גמרא is using against שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'beginning' is when he saw the event, and the 'end' is when he testifies in court. What happens in between does not matter. A witness who went blind and stays blind is unfit at the 'end,' so by this rule he is פסול, against שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: His beginning: when he saw the event

steps.whatToRemember: A witness must be fit both when he sees the event and when he testifies. Being unfit in between doesn't matter. This ברייתא seems to directly contradict שמואל's ruling that a blind witness can testify about land.
steps.confusionAlert: Watch the small words. To be פסול, being unfit at EITHER time ('or') is enough. To be כשר, he must be fit at BOTH times ('and').

phrases.english: This is the rule:
anyone whose beginning or end
is in a state of disqualification is disqualified;
if his beginning and end are both in a state of fitness, he is fit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Wraps up the ברייתא's cases with one general principle.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling (step 11), and by extension רב ששת (step 12) and רב פפא (step 13).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A witness who stays blind is unfit at the 'end,' so by the ברייתא's rule he is פסול even for land.
